readerTitle: Ask for the next small step, not the sale
caseNote: 가상 사례 2개 (지역 소규모 회계 대행사, 가정 청소 업체) + 가상 적용 (피트니스 스튜디오용 예약 소프트웨어) · 수치와 결과는 모두 설명용
insight: 콜 투 액션은 '구매하라'는 외침이 아니다. 고객이 지금 감당할 수 있는 가장 작은 다음 행동 하나를 크기와 결과까지 분명하게 알려주는 문장이다.
misconception: '문의하세요'면 충분하다. 버튼과 선택지를 많이 둘수록 연락이 더 많이 온다.

sources.text: 마케팅 실무의 일반 원리 (명확한 단일 행동 요청, 고객 준비 단계에 맞춘 요청)
모든 사례와 결과는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 회계 대행사, 청소 업체, 배관공, 예약 소프트웨어 사례는 모두 가상입니다. 전환율 등 구체적 수치는 일부러 넣지 않았습니다. 게시 전 카드에 수치가 추가되지 않았는지 확인하세요.
6번 카드 softwareNote의 '소규모 팀에는 무료 체험, 대기업에는 데모 예약'은 많은 B2B 소프트웨어 사이트에서 보이는 일반적 관행으로만 서술했습니다. 특정 기업 사례로 바꾸려면 출처를 추가하세요.
'선택지가 많을수록 결정을 미룬다'는 주장은 일반 원리로만 표현했습니다. 잼 연구 등 재현성 논란이 있는 연구는 인용하지 않았습니다 (CUS-10-06 참고).

cards.title: Two businesses, one missing line
body: A bookkeeping firm and a house-cleaning company both have plenty of people reading about them. Very few ever get in touch.
Their services are good. Their prices are fair. The problem sits at the very end: the line that tells people what to do next.

image.label: A website and a flyer, each ending in a blank line
image.brief: 왼쪽에 회계 사무소 웹페이지, 오른쪽에 청소 업체 전단지. 둘 다 내용은 꽉 차 있는데 맨 아래 한 줄만 빈칸으로 점선 처리되어 있음. 독자가 그 앞에서 머뭇거리다 돌아서는 작은 사람 실루엣. 실제 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Your website ends with one line.
body: You run a small bookkeeping firm for local businesses. Owners read your services page, seem interested, then leave.
You're rewriting the last line on the page. Which should it be?

options.feedback: Safe and polite, but it leaves the work to the reader: what to ask, how long it takes, whether they'll get a sales pitch. Most people put that off.

options.text: "Book a free 20-minute review of last month's books"
options.feedback: One action, a known size and something useful in return. You lose people who only want to browse, but those who act are ready to talk.

options.text: "Call, email, download our brochure or follow us"
options.feedback: More doors feel like more chances. But each option is another decision, and many readers decide later. A brochure can work as a quieter second option.

cards.title: Same service. Different ask.
body: The firm swapped "Contact us" for the 20-minute review. Owners now knew what they would do, how long it would take and what they would get.
The cleaning company changed its flyer too. "Call for a quote" became "Text your postcode and number of rooms. Get a price in 10 minutes." People who dislike phone calls could now ask in seconds.
Neither business changed what it sold. Both changed **what they asked for**.

image.label: Before and after: vague ask versus specific ask
image.brief: 두 칸 비교. 왼쪽 'Before'에는 흐릿한 회색 글씨 "Contact us", "Call for a quote". 오른쪽 'After'에는 선명한 글씨 "Book a free 20-minute review", "Text your postcode, get a price in 10 minutes". 오른쪽 문구 옆에 시계 아이콘과 작은 발걸음 아이콘. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Call to action
body: A **call to action** is the line that tells someone exactly what to do next, and what happens when they do.
Good ones share three things: one action, a clear size (time, money or effort), and a reason to do it now instead of later.
Vague asks like "Learn more" aren't wrong. They just leave the reader to plan the next step alone, and most people won't.

cards.title: Take one apart.
body: A plumber's version: *"Text a photo of the leak. Get a price within an hour."* Each piece removes one reason to wait.

breakdown.label: The action
breakdown.detail: One verb, one thing to do

breakdown.label: The size
breakdown.detail: Small enough to do right now

breakdown.label: What they get
breakdown.detail: Useful even if they don't hire you

breakdown.label: What happens next
breakdown.detail: No guessing, no waiting by the phone

cards.title: Ask for the next step, not the final one.
body: A first-time reader rarely signs up for a year of bookkeeping. They might give you 20 minutes. Match the ask to **how ready** the person is.
Urgency changes the answer. Someone with water on the kitchen floor is ready now, so "Call now, we answer 24/7" fits. Someone choosing an accountant needs a smaller, safer first step.
cards.softwareNote: This is why many software sites offer "Start free trial" to small teams and "Book a demo" to large companies. Each step matches how much the buyer has at risk.

cards.title: A clear promise must be kept.
body: A specific ask raises the stakes on follow-through. If you promise a price in 10 minutes, someone has to answer in 10 minutes.
A very easy step can also attract people who were never going to buy. Free reviews cost staff time, so watch who books them.
And skip fake urgency. "Only 2 spots left" when it isn't true trades one quick click for lost trust.

cards.title: Now it's a software company.
body: You sell scheduling software for fitness studios. Your most-read article is "How to plan a weekly class timetable." Readers are studio owners who found it through search.
What should the article end with?

options.feedback: A big step for someone who met you five minutes ago. A few serious buyers will book; most readers will simply leave.
Clear and small, but generic. It doesn't connect to what the reader came for, so it reads like a sales pitch.

options.text: "Copy this timetable into a free account. Takes 2 minutes."
options.feedback: It continues the job the reader came to do and shows the product solving their own problem. The trade-off: it feels less like a full commitment, so some may stop there.

cards.title: Make the next small step obvious.
body: A good call to action names one action, how small it is and what the person gets. Ask for the step they're ready for, not the sale you want.
**Try it today:** read the last line of your website, flyer or proposal. Could a stranger tell what to do, how long it takes and what happens next? If not, rewrite it.
